name: Postliberalism
summary: Postliberalism holds that liberalism's picture of the person as a self-interested chooser has dissolved families, communities and shared ends, leaving a market and a state with nothing between them. It seeks to rebuild intermediary institutions (family, local government, unions, associations), to orient politics and law to a substantive common good and a fixed human nature, and to replace market individualism with economic reciprocity. Its strands differ: Deneen's localist and Christian critique, Pabst's British associational political economy, and the American legal programme of common good constitutionalism.
scope: Political postliberalism as set out by Patrick Deneen's 'Unsustainable Liberalism' (2012), Adrian Pabst's 'Postliberalism: the new centre-ground of British politics' (2017) and Conor Casey and Adrian Vermeule's 'Myths of Common Good Constitutionalism' (2022). It excludes postliberal theology, Catholic integralism as a separate entry, and the later books of these authors, which were not read. Where the three differ in emphasis (a strong executive and no fixed institutional form for Casey and Vermeule, devolution and associations for Pabst and Deneen) the answer is mixed or limited to what each shared.

furtherReading.title: Patrick Deneen, Unsustainable Liberalism (First Things, 2012)
furtherReading.note: The short essay that sets out the postliberal critique of liberal autonomy and consumption.

furtherReading.title: Adrian Pabst, Postliberalism: the new centre-ground of British politics (Kent Academic Repository)
furtherReading.note: A readable account of postliberal economics and society in Britain.

furtherReading.title: Casey and Vermeule, Myths of Common Good Constitutionalism (Harvard JLPP, 2022)
furtherReading.note: The legal side of postliberalism, defended against its critics.

sources.title: Unsustainable Liberalism
sources.author: Patrick J. Deneen (First Things, Aug/Sept 2012)
sources.usedFor: Liberty as self-government, family and community, consumption, limits to growth, human nature, federalism.

sources.title: Postliberalism: the new centre-ground of British politics (Political Quarterly 88(3), 2017)
sources.author: Adrian Pabst
sources.usedFor: Economic justice, intermediary institutions, trade, the state, populism and the left-right divide.

sources.title: Myths of Common Good Constitutionalism (Harvard Journal of Law and Public Policy 45, 2022)
sources.author: Conor Casey and Adrian Vermeule
sources.usedFor: Common good, law and virtue, rights, regime forms, executive power, subsidiarity.

class-collaboration.rationale: Pabst favours reciprocity and mutual benefit between employers and workers in a continental model of company governance and in shared associations.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Pabst describes the High Tory tradition he favours as marked by mutual assistance and support of the needy, and does not ask for welfare cuts.

decide-locally.rationale: Deneen urges a more robust federalism with local self-government, Pabst wants devolved and regional government, and Casey and Vermeule hold that public authority must respect subsidiary bodies; none sets "as locally as possible" as an absolute.

democracy-best.rationale: Pabst defends popular participation, but Casey and Vermeule hold that parliamentary, presidential, monarchical and republican systems alike can be ordered to the common good, so democracy has no special rank.

direct-votes.rationale: Pabst condemns the plebiscite populism of the hard left and radical right as locking politics into theatrics and oligarchy, and prefers representation through intermediary bodies.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Deneen contrasts voluntarist rights with obligations to community, present and future, and Pabst stresses mutual obligation; Casey and Vermeule define rights by the common good but keep them as real limits, so the ranking is not stated flatly.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Pabst reports with approval that May's government might block sales of strategic firms to asset-stripping foreign buyers, without stating a general rule.

free-trade.rationale: Pabst says unrestricted global free trade is likely to hurt the workers a post-liberal politics defends, and prefers regional agreements as a third way between free trade and protection.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Casey and Vermeule say what is due, in the classical account of rights, is due to individuals, families and associations, and Pabst gives intermediary institutions agency.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Pabst argues politics is moving away from left-right toward a divide over progressive liberalism, and that post-liberalism combines paradoxical pairs such as fiscal discipline with economic justice.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Pabst rejects both rampant market capitalism and the statist economy of the hard left, and Deneen sees left and right closing a pincer of one state and one market.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Casey and Vermeule assign public authority the aims of economic justice, public goods, a healthy culture and curbing vice, and Pabst wants an active state at the service of society.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Pabst calls for greater popular participation, more worker involvement in running companies and devolved government as shared goals of post-liberalism.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Pabst makes shared identity, patriotism and inherited ways of life central to post-liberal politics, and Deneen values culture that hands on the wisdom of the past.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Pabst backs reforms that change the nature of the market, such as aligning executive pay with long-term performance and the interests of employees and consumers, and criticises weak control of finance.

single-common-good.rationale: Casey and Vermeule make law and politics answer to one common good and reject balancing interests, while Pabst speaks of a "balance of interests" within shared goals, so the strands differ in emphasis.

social-market-economy.rationale: Pabst says the test of post-liberalism is forging a social market that avoids both liberal economics and liberal statism, with state and market embedded in civil society.

state-as-business.rationale: Pabst criticises the market-state that remakes social institutions as replicas of business enterprises, and May's line "we don't hate the state" is cited with approval.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Pabst welcomes an active state supplying patient capital and industrial strategy, while criticising how narrowly the 2017 strategy was drawn; no principle of state direction is stated.

state-harmful.rationale: Casey and Vermeule hold the common good's conditions cannot be secured without public authority, and Pabst says "we value the role that only the state can play"; Deneen looks to a shrinking but still constitutional state.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Pabst accepts selective and temporary protection for some sectors but warns that protectionism has almost always fed inter-state conflict, so his own position is mixed.

total-state.rationale: Pabst says post-liberalism puts society above state and market and criticises extremes that centralise state power against the freedom to associate, while Casey and Vermeule make the state's educative role subsidiary to family and community.

traditional-family.rationale: Deneen laments the fading of stable lifelong marriage and counts the family among the constitutive institutions, Pabst stresses families as a basis of social life, and Casey and Vermeule list promoting marriage and stable family life among the common good's conditions.

unions-good.rationale: Pabst names trade unions among the intermediary institutions that give people agency and wants them embedded in the economy.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Pabst argues the two liberalisms concentrate political and economic power in small groups and so hollow out democracy and society.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Pabst favours workers' representatives on company boards, profit-sharing businesses and a more continental model of company governance.

missingStatements.text: Judges should read a constitution in light of the common good and natural law, not only the meaning its text had when enacted.
missingStatements.rationale: Casey and Vermeule argue that classical legal interpretation reads enacted texts as reasoned determinations ordered to the common good and reject originalism as the sole method.

notes: Strands: Deneen is localist and Christian, Pabst writes of a British associational economy (worker board representation, regional banks, social market), and Casey and Vermeule are agnostic on institutional form while favouring robust executive government. Answers rest only on these three texts; later books such as Deneen's Regime Change were not read. Themes searched in the texts: economy, government, society, liberty, culture, ecology, technology and trade; world, means and globalism themes are largely silent. 2026-11-05 (Brandon): 25 answers resting only on sources that never discuss Postliberalism (borrowing: Unsustainable Liberalism; Myths of Common Good Constitutionalism) were cleared to null.
